deep.reconstruction:
The page has drawings only, apart from a few labels. They are on the back of a 1982 IBM JES2 listing ("DATASETS PICTURES"). It belongs to the 1983-84 notes on systems of pseudo-lines, i.e. arrangements of pseudolines in the real projective plane P^2(R).

(1) Top left: the neighbourhood of one pseudoline.
- A distinguished pseudoline (yellow-green) runs through a thin strip bounded by two brown curves.
- The bottom brown curve carries the labels p, q, r, t, u, w, x, z; the top one carries p', q', s', u', v', w', y', z'.
- In P^2 a regular neighbourhood of a pseudoline is a Möbius band, whose boundary is one circle running twice around. So the primed and unprimed labels plausibly name the two lifts, or two sides, of the same boundary arcs and cells. They can be identified after the half-twist.
- The other pseudolines (orange) cross the strip in pairs that form an X. Each X's crossing lies either on the green line (one is marked with a dot: a triple point) or just above or below it (forming a small triangle with it).
- Thick dark bars on the brown curves mark the boundary edges cut out between consecutive crossings.
- The small marks 'x' and '3' at the crossings seem to classify the local configurations. '3' plausibly marks triangular cells adjacent to the green line. This would fit Levi's classical theorem that in a simple arrangement each pseudoline borders at least 3 triangles.

(2) Top right: the disc model of P^2.
- A circle, with antipodal boundary points identified, is crossed by orange pseudolines.
- Blue bars on the boundary and small X's outside the circle at top and bottom indicate how strands are glued, or cross, "at infinity" under the antipodal identification.

(3) Bottom right: the barycentric subdivision of a single cell.
- The cell is a polygon with a blue boundary.
- Green segments run from the centre to the vertices; orange segments run from the centre to the edge midpoints.
- Dashed brown triangles near the boundary mark individual flags (vertex, edge, face).

(4) Centre right: local pieces of the flag graph, coloured by the type of generator.
- An H, an X-shape with a dark middle edge, a Y, a broken path, and a comb with orange legs and dark green tops.
- Together with the boxed list "σ1, σ, σ2, σ0", this is Grothendieck's cartographic formalism from his theory of maps. Flags are permuted by the involutions σ0 (change vertex), σ1 (change edge), σ2 (change face), with (σ0σ2)^2 = 1, giving the cartographic group C2.
- The extra "σ" is plausibly an involution adapted to pseudoline arrangements. Examples would be the "go straight through a 4-valent vertex" operation or the switch between the two sides of a pseudoline; this is unsure.
- So the page appears to encode an arrangement as a non-orientable map on P^2, with an extra involution recording the pseudoline structure.

(5) Pencil sketches: many lines through one point with arrows, and a point surrounded by lens-shaped petals (labelled 2).
- These show the local structure at a multiple point and its perturbation (simplification) into small digons and triangles.
- Alternatively they show the link and flag structure around a vertex.

Purpose: a combinatorial, map-theoretic description of pseudoline arrangements. It covers the neighbourhood of a line, the gluing at infinity, the flag decomposition of cells and the generators acting on flags, presumably toward classifying or enumerating such systems.
errors: No explicit claims to check; drawings only. The meaning of the 'x' and '3' marks and of the unsubscripted σ is not determinable from this page alone.

ideas.what: Regular neighbourhood of a pseudoline in P^2 as a strip (Möbius band) whose two boundary sides carry paired labels (p/p', q/q', ...)
ideas.modern_name: Möbius-band neighbourhood of a pseudoline; zone of a line in an arrangement
ideas.usually_credited_to: Levi (1926); zone theory: Edelsbrunner et al. (1980s)

ideas.what: Counting or marking triangles adjacent to a given pseudoline ('3' marks)
ideas.modern_name: Levi's triangle theorem (each line of a simple arrangement borders ≥3 triangles)

ideas.what: Barycentric subdivision of cells into flags, with involutions σ0, σ1, σ2 acting on flags (flag graph coloured by generator)
ideas.modern_name: Cartographic group C2 / flag graph of a map (incl. non-orientable maps)
ideas.where_published: Esquisse d'un programme (1984), section on combinatorial maps / cartographic groups

ideas.what: Applying the cartographic formalism to arrangements of pseudolines on P^2, with an additional involution σ
ideas.modern_name: Arrangements as 4-valent maps on RP^2 / combinatorial encodings of rank-3 oriented matroids via flags
ideas.usually_credited_to: Folkman–Lawrence 1978 (topological representation); Goodman–Pollack (allowable sequences); flag-based encodings in maps literature

missed.claim: Grothendieck applies his cartographic-group / flag-involution formalism (σ0, σ1, σ2 plus an extra σ) to pseudoline arrangements on P^2. That would give a group-theoretic encoding of rank-3 oriented matroids within the same framework as dessins and maps. The literature treats these two areas largely separately.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: An explicit 'cartographic' presentation of pseudoline arrangements could link the enumeration and classification of oriented matroids to the Galois-action and moduli viewpoint on maps. This page alone does not show it was carried through.

deep.surprise_reason: These are standard pseudoline-arrangement sketches. The only notable feature is the explicit use of Esquisse-style flag involutions, with an extra σ, in the arrangement context: a plausible but undeveloped bridge, documented here only pictorially.
transcription_corrections: Bottom row of labels on the strip: p, q, r, t, u, w, x, z. The final '2' near the lower right of the strip is the letter z, matching z' above.
The small marks at the crossings are 'x' (and '^'-like ticks) and '3' (possibly 'ʒ'); they are attached to individual crossings, not a separate row.
Big '2' in pencil above the petal (lens) figure at lower left-centre.
Boxed text reads 'σ1, σ, σ2, σ0' (σ without a subscript in second position).
